Row counts are today's live counts, read only. Rows that a fold moves into a table are listed as moved in, not added, because the migration merges, filters or expires some of them.

tables.name: agent_loops
tables.holds: One row per org-graph node that has a standing loop: when it started, the last tick, the day's tick count, the no-progress streak and whether the loop is paused or waiting.
tables.kept_how_long: until the node's loop setting is removed
tables.note: Area changed from machines to org-graph: node is a graph node. The Graph tab node card shows a Loop block (tui/map_card.go).

tables.name: agents
tables.holds: One agent of the org tree: a named role (coding agent, bot, lead) with its team (`team_id`), its pinned lead session (`lead_session`), its explicit lead-level grant (`lead_level`), and a tombstone flag when it is retired. `agents.lead_session` and `agents.lead_level` are the single source for an agent's lead session and explicit lead-level grant.
tables.kept_how_long: Forever (a retired agent is only flagged as tombstoned).
tables.core_why: The lasting identity behind sessions; charters and leads hang on it.

tables.name: app_tokens
tables.holds: One row per hashed access or refresh token of a connected app, with its type, expiry, token family and the time it was used.
tables.kept_how_long: access tokens 1 hour, refresh tokens 90 days, used refresh hashes 90 days; swept every 10 minutes; at most 20 access tokens per app
tables.note: Also the source of the refresh-rotation count (rotations of a family in the last 24 hours).

tables.name: apps
tables.holds: One row per connected app (phone, bot or other client), and, after the fold, per registered sign-in client waiting for approval: name, kind, OAuth client id and name, redirect addresses, grant and response types, token auth method, source, state, when created, last used and revoked, and what it is granted.
tables.kept_how_long: for ever; a revoked app is only marked revoked
tables.note: Planned by the Apps and sign-in rework, which is still being written. Rows in state registered are not connected apps and are never shown as such.

tables.name: ask_sorts
tables.holds: One sort decision the chief of staff made on an ask (answer, route, merge, close), with what it replaced so it can be undone.
tables.kept_how_long: for ever

tables.name: charter_drafts
tables.holds: One charter value that a session drafted from the project AGENTS.md (`pending`, `accepted`, `rejected`, `superseded`), or an `asked` marker (`status='asked'`, `source_hash`, `asked_at`) so a session is not asked twice for the same source text.
tables.kept_how_long: Forever (the status changes to accepted or rejected, the row stays; the `asked` row is replaced when the source text changes).

tables.name: charter_values
tables.holds: One charter setting (a rule or text) for a level (global, team, agent or repo), a scope and an attribute, with who set it and when.
tables.kept_how_long: until the value is cleared, undone, or its repo is removed
tables.note: Audit text updated: levels agent and repo were folded in from agent_charter and graph_charter. Repo rows are deleted by RemoveArchitect.

tables.name: deliveries
tables.holds: One row per delivery state change of a message (stored, delivered, failed and so on) with detail text and time.
tables.kept_how_long: for ever by default (--keep-messages is 0); when set, deleted with their messages by the hourly prune
tables.shown_note: Shown only as the state and detail line of a message.

tables.name: delivery_changes
tables.holds: One row per change (a branch of work) that a worker or session has submitted for delivery, with its project, branch, title, current state and merged commit.
tables.kept_how_long: for ever
tables.core_why: One row per change under delivery; all step tables hang on it.

tables.name: delivery_evidence
tables.holds: One row per report on a delivery step (accept, review, test, merge, release or verify) of a change: the result, who reported it, which model, and a note.
tables.kept_how_long: for ever, the database refuses to update or delete these rows
tables.note: Append-only: triggers abort UPDATE and DELETE.

tables.name: delivery_retries
tables.holds: One row per message that is waiting to be delivered again, with the number of attempts so far and the time of the next try.
tables.kept_how_long: until the message is delivered, answered, expired or withdrawn
tables.shown_note: The retry loop (RunRetries) reads it; no tab or tool lists it.
tables.note: Area corrected from delivery: it is about message delivery, not the delivery pipeline. Rows are also deleted in storeMessage, expireMessage, withdrawOne, StoreHandoff and removeFromBatch.

tables.name: delivery_revisions
tables.holds: One row per revision of a change (each time the branch is pushed again), with its commit and, since the fold, the size of the diff, the risk signals and the hand-back check result.
tables.kept_how_long: for ever
tables.note: Audit text was only 'each revision'; diff_stat, signals and handback_check come from the folded delivery_revision_stats.

tables.name: delivery_step_tasks
tables.holds: One row per open delivery step of a change that needs someone to do it: who owns it, who claimed it, and when it was last nudged or is waiting. It also holds the notices sent for the step (`notices`, a map from a session to the notice message) and the agents that may approve it when it is delegated (`delegates`).
tables.kept_how_long: Until the step is reported, closed, retired or its change ends. A done step keeps no task: its row in `delivery_evidence` is the record.
tables.core_why: The state of each delivery step of each change.

tables.name: desk_log
tables.holds: One log line about something that happened on the Desk (an ask sorted, a permission applied), with what undoes it.
tables.kept_how_long: The newest 2000 lines, trimmed on every 200th insert.

tables.name: events
tables.holds: One row per gateway event in the audit log: time, kind, machine, session, message and a detail line.
tables.kept_how_long: 90 days, pruned hourly
tables.note: Events are read through query.events; the Messages tab feed and the Graph tab talk feed use them. Area kept as messages although it is a general audit log.
tables.core_why: The audit log that every operation writes to.

tables.name: findings
tables.holds: One finding reported about a model or a harness. Enough findings promote a playbook note.

tables.name: follow_ups
tables.holds: One row per follow-up check set by a message sender or the chief: the event expected (reply, change, conversation, session), who waits, the due time and whether it is pending, met or raised.

journeys.title: Send a message and get a reply
journeys.summary: A message is checked, stored, handed to the receiver's machine, confirmed as delivered, and later closed by the receiver's reply.

steps.what: The gateway checks that the sending session really lives on the machine that sent the request.
It looks for an earlier message with the same sender and idempotency key, so a retry never stores the message twice.
It checks that the receiving session exists and follows it to the session that replaced it, if it was replaced.
It reads which session is the CTO, because the CTO only accepts replies and requests from lead agents.
For a request, it looks up the owner's rule between the two projects: normal, ask first, or never.
It counts the messages already in this conversation to enforce the conversation limit.
The new message is saved with state 'stored', its conversation, its expiry time and its sender and receiver.
If the owner's last prompt to the sender explains this first request, the message keeps it in messages.owner_prompt, and the sender's copy on sessions is cleared, so the prompt is used once.
The audit log records 'msg.stored' with the type, receiver and size (never the text).
Just before sending to the receiver's machine, the message state moves from 'stored' to 'dispatched'.
The audit log records 'msg.dispatched' for the receiver.
The receiver's daemon reports back, and the gateway keeps that report as one delivery row.
The message state moves to 'delivered' (it stays 'replied' or 'failed' if it already was).
When a message is delivered between two projects that have no link yet, the gateway reads the messages those projects exchanged in the last 7 days, as evidence that they talk.
The audit log records 'msg.delivered' for the receiver.
The receiver's reply is saved as a new message in the same conversation, and in the same transaction the original request is marked 'replied'.
Any pending retry for the answered request is deleted, because it no longer needs delivering.
An open 'owed answer' reminder for the request is closed as replied.

journeys.notes: Normal path only. If the receiver is offline, dispatch calls wakeForMessage instead of delivering at once and the message waits as 'stored'. If the owner's rule is 'ask', the message is saved with state 'held' and an ask is opened (openHeldAsk) before anything is sent. If the gateway cannot write to the receiver's machine, the state goes back to 'stored'. The reply goes through the same msg.send path as the request, so it also writes its own 'msg.stored' event and then the same dispatch, deliveries, delivered and events steps to the original sender; that second round is not repeated above. A reply that carries an outcome (accept, reject, escalate, redirect) also writes graph_outcomes, and a reject or escalate also writes inbox_items. A request to a busy session may be held at the gateway (messages.held_for_busy) until the session is ready. An ack (no body) closes the request without any delivery.

journeys.title: Start a worker and get its hand-back
journeys.summary: The picker reads the machine, quota, past results and prices to choose a model, the worker starts and runs, and its hand-back and run record reach the starter.

steps.what: The gateway looks up the project folders registered on each machine, to find where the worker can run (project folders seen in sessions are read too).
It reads the machine's state: online, accepts workers, which agent tools are installed, and each tool's models.
It reads quota windows that this machine already learned are used up, so the picker does not choose a provider that is blocked (live quota readings come from memory, not the database).
It reads the owner's picker settings: registered worker profiles, model scores, minimum scores per difficulty, allowed and protected providers, floors, and the rotation counter.
steps.source: internal/gateway/workers.go:workerStart -> worker_profiles.go:WorkerProfiles, scores.go:scores, difficultyMinimums, workerProviders, protectedProviders, workerFloors; worker_rotation.go:WorkerRotation

steps.what: It reads the price of each model, so the picker can compare the expected cost per accepted result.
It reads the track record of past worker runs (complete, partial, failed, fixes needed) per model, which scores each model on tasks of this difficulty.
It reads the difficulty the judge gave to past tasks, to place each past run in the right difficulty bucket.
It reads the tokens past runs used, to turn token counts into a cost per run.
It reads which models recently failed or lost sign-in on this machine, to skip models that are cooling down.
The rotation counter is saved, so the next start spreads work across models instead of always picking the same one.
The gateway records the start (reference, machine, who asked, project, harness, permissions, the 'done' list) before it asks the machine to launch.
The judge's difficulty result and the picker's explanation are saved under the new worker session.
One row per candidate model is saved: its score, cost, quota room, chance of being picked, and why it was skipped or chosen.
The audit log records 'worker.started' with project, harness, model and who started it.
At a complete hand-back, the worker's branch is submitted as a change to deliver (a first revision row is saved with it).
The hand-back notice is saved as a reply to the starter's task message, and the task is marked 'replied'. It is delivered to the starter like any message.
When the worker stops, its run is saved: model, outcome, seconds, files and lines changed, fixes, and struggle counters. This feeds the track record the picker reads next time.
The tokens the worker used are saved with the run, so its cost can be computed later.

journeys.notes: Normal automatic pick, successful launch, complete hand-back. Real reads and writes that are left out to stay within 18 steps: sessions is read to check the caller and its running workers (workerStart, withQuotaBurn) and to find provider limits reported by live sessions (choose.go:providerLimits); sessions is written when the new worker session registers (session.upsert, store.go:upsertSession) and when the run ends (SetWorkerSessionEnded sets status 'ended'); worker_starts is updated twice more (startSession stores the session id, closeStart marks the start 'closed'); the project's worker permission is read from setting_values and setting_revision (store_policy.go:WorkerPermissions); delivery_changes is read to warn about overlapping briefs (brief_check.go:openChangeBriefs); playbook is read for model notes (track.go:PlaybookForChoice); the brief itself goes to the worker as a msg.send with the worker-task flag (daemon/operator.go), so it also writes messages, events and deliveries as in the message journey. At hand-back the daemon also asks worker_rate_offers whether to ask the starter for a rating (ratings.go:OfferRate writes one row); worker.stopped also writes model_failures (success_at, RecordModelSuccess) and closes the worker's open inbox_items; the judge result may arrive later from the machine (worker.assessment) and refreshes the cached picker table. worker_ratings is written only if the starter rates the worker with agent_worker_rate, and worker_defects only when a defect is reported later. The picker table and price book are cached in memory and rebuilt from worker_runs, worker_assessments, worker_usage and model_prices after relevant writes, so the picker reads above happen when the cache is rebuilt, not on every start. If a launch fails the gate moves to the next candidate without a new pick. A refused start writes only an 'worker.refused' event.

journeys.title: A machine connects and reports health
journeys.summary: A machine enrolls once with a code, then on each connection proves its token, says hello with its health and tools, syncs its sessions, and is marked silent if it drops without a reason.

steps.what: On first setup, the invite (a nodes row in state invited) is checked and marked used, so it cannot be used again.
A new machine row is created with its name, operating system and the hash of its secret token (the token itself is never stored).
The audit log records 'node.enrolled' with the machine's host name.
On every connection, the gateway checks that the machine was not removed and that its token hash matches.
The hello is stored on the machine row: host name, version, last seen time, whether it accepts workers, time zone, Tailscale address, and whether it supports graph references.
steps.source: internal/gateway/server.go:handle (case hello) -> nodes.go:SetNodeHello, SetNodeLaunch, SetNodeTimeZone, SetNodeTailscaleIP; graph_refs.go:SetNodeGraphRefs

steps.what: The machine's health report (restart time, load and similar) replaces the previous one, with the time it arrived.
The list of installed agent tools (Claude, Codex, and so on) with versions, models and sign-in state is saved. The same write is repeated later when the machine sends node.harnesses.
If the tool list changed, the audit log records 'node.harnesses' with what changed.
The machine is marked as back: any open outage (dropped, asleep, silent) is cleared.
The audit log records 'node.connected' with the remote address.
The machine lists its agent sessions. Each is added or updated, and sessions the gateway thought were online but are missing from the list are marked offline.
When the link drops, the last time a frame arrived is saved, and the time of the drop starts a possible outage (unless the machine announced it was going to sleep).
The audit log records 'node.disconnected'.
After the offline grace period, every session of that machine is marked offline, and ended workers are marked 'ended'.
If the outage stays unexplained for the silence limit, the machine is marked silent. The once-a-minute check does this.
A silent machine is queued for the CTO with the text '<host> went silent ... it may be hung' (it is not sent to the owner).

journeys.notes: The first four steps are split by time: steps 1 to 3 happen once, when a machine first joins with an enrollment code; later connections start at step 4. A removed machine is refused at step 4 (HTTP 410). Steps 5 to 9 are the hello frame handled by the gateway; each is its own UPDATE on the nodes row. Live usage and quota reports (node.usage) are kept in memory only and write no table. Later node.harnesses frames repeat steps 6 to 8 without a new connection. If the machine sends a sleep report (node.sleep or sleeps inside hello), NodeSlept updates the nodes silence columns, and, if the outage was already silent, closes its open ask and its cto_intake item; step 9 does the same when the machine returns after being silent. The order of steps 16 to 18 depends on timers: the offline grace period moves sessions offline, and the silence limit (checked every minute) marks the machine silent. A silent machine that later returns has its cto_intake item closed by NodeLinkUp.

journeys.title: A change from accept to release
journeys.summary: An agent hands in a change, the delivery steps open one after another, each step is claimed and reported with evidence, and the change ends as done.

steps.what: The gateway checks that the session handing in the change really lives on the machine that is calling.
It reads the delivery rules for this repo (which tests, who approves the merge, review settings) to build the pipeline of steps.
It reads the org graph links that name the owner of each step (accepts, reviews, tests, approves, merges, releases, verifies). A step with no link is owned by the caller.
A new change row is stored with the branch, the head commit, the caller and the state open. A second submit on the same branch updates this row instead.
The head commit is recorded as revision 1. A new head later adds revision 2, 3 and so on, and starts the steps again.
The first ready step (accept) gets a task row that names its owner. Steps that need an earlier step wait.
A notice 'you have a step to claim' is stored for the session that owns the step.
The notice id is saved in the step task's notices, so it can be cancelled when the step is claimed, finished or replaced.
A line 'Sent step ... of change ... to a session' is added to the Desk log.
The owner session claims the step (agent_step_claim). The task now shows who works on it, and nobody else can report it.
When the step is reported (agent_step_report), the task is marked completed under the same session.
The result (pass, fail or needs owner), the commit, the fields and who did the work are stored as evidence. Evidence is never edited, a newer report just wins.
The gateway reads all evidence, finds which steps are now ready, and opens the next task (review, test, approve, merge, release, verify in turn).
For a step owned by the merger, the gateway looks up which session is the merger for this repo on this machine, and only that session may claim the step.
For an approve step set to delegated, the repo lead and the team lead (found from the repo and team tables) are listed as the sessions allowed to approve. The caller is never its own approver.
For an approve step that needs the owner's written approval, an Inbox item is created and linked to the step, revision and commit.
A passing merge report moves the change to merged and stores the merged commit. When every step after merge has passed, the state becomes done (a close report makes it stopped).
When the change is done or stopped, the open asks about it are closed so nothing stale stays on the Desk.

journeys.notes: Normal path: with the default rules every step is owned by the caller, so steps 14, 15 and 16 do not happen. Step 14 (project_mergers) happens only when the repo assigns the merge step to the merger. Step 15 (delivery_step_delegates) happens only when the merge or deploy approval rule is delegated. Step 16 (delivery_step_inbox) happens only when the approval rule needs the owner's written approval; the owner's answer then goes through answerDeliveryApproval (internal/gateway/delivery_approval.go): it reads delivery_step_inbox, writes delivery_evidence with by=owner, updates inbox_items and writes standing_orders (the answer is kept as an owner judgment), then queueSteps opens the next step. I could not establish from the code which approval rule is the default, because it depends on the repo maturity. A new head commit on the same branch bumps the revision: old open step approvals in inbox_items are dismissed and the steps start again on the new revision. A needs_owner report also creates an inbox_items row (syncStepAsk). Step tasks are also re-sent as reminders by dispatchStepTasks. Evidence is only read for the next-step decision (queueSteps reads delivery_evidence). The audit table events gets no row from this path, except when several nudges to one session are merged into one batch message (nudge_batch.go:combineNudges). delivery_retries and deliveries belong to message delivery, not to the change. The wire entry is the frames change.submit, step.claim and step.report handled in handleDelivery (internal/gateway/delivery_changes.go).

journeys.title: The chief of staff sorts an ask
journeys.summary: An agent asks the owner a question, it becomes an Inbox item that the chief of staff sorts, the Desk shows it, the owner answers, and the answer goes back to the asker.

steps.what: The gateway checks the asking session is on the calling machine and finds its repo and display name.
It reads which session is the chief of staff, then decides if the ask goes to the chief or straight to the owner.
It looks for an open ask, or one closed in the last 10 minutes, that asks the same thing, so a repeat joins it instead of making a duplicate.
A new open ask is stored with the question, the options, the recommendation and who handles it next (the chief).
Every few seconds the gateway collects the asks waiting for the chief and bundles those that arrived close together.
One message listing the asks to sort is stored for the chief of staff session.
Each ask in the batch is marked as sent to the chief, so it is not sent twice.
The chief searches the owner's earlier decisions and rules (agent_owner_judgments_find) to see if the owner already decided this kind of question.
When the chief calls agent_ask_sort, the gateway reads the ask and checks that the caller is the live chief.
For the result 'owner', the ask gets its priority, the reason why only the owner can decide, and next_who set to the owner.
The sort is recorded with who sorted, the result, the reason and the previous state, so it can be shown and undone.
A line 'Chief sent ask to you (priority N): ...' is added to the Desk log.
The Desk reads the asks that are open and waiting for the owner.
The Desk also reads the latest log lines, newest first.
The owner answers in the TUI. The ask is marked answered (or approved or refused) with the answer text and time.
The question and the owner's answer are saved as an owner judgment, so the chief can find it the next time (step 8).
The answer is stored as a message for the asking session, and for every session that joined the ask as a repeat. The gateway then delivers it.

journeys.notes: Normal path: the chief sorts the ask to the owner. Other results of agent_ask_sort: close or merge (inbox_items status closed, the chief answer is the asker's reply), send (next_who becomes another session and a message is stored for it), withdraw, confirm and picker (held worker starts). If no chief is live, createInboxItem sets next_who to the owner and steps 5 to 11 do not happen. If the chief cites a standing rule (rule field), SortAskWith also reads standing_orders in ruleApplies (internal/gateway/desk_rules.go) and writes rule_id on ask_sorts. If the owner answers with a scope, a standing rule is added to standing_orders and a line to desk_log in the same transaction (addRuleTx). A repeat from another session joins the open ask instead of making a new row (joinItem). The events table gets no row on this path in the code I read. I did not trace the daemon and MCP hops (agent_owner_ask to the gateway frame inbox.create) beyond the gateway handler in internal/gateway/server.go.

journeys.title: The owner changes a charter or a setting
journeys.summary: A charter attribute or a setting is written with a new revision and a history row, and readers pick it up from the store or from a push to every daemon.

steps.what: For a repo charter, the gateway checks the repo exists and is not archived (for an agent charter it checks the agents table the same way).
It reads the current value of this attribute, so an unchanged value writes nothing.
The new value is stored for the level (global, team, repo or agent), the scope and the attribute, with time and author. An empty value deletes the row.
A history row keeps the old value, the new value, the author and the time. Its id is the revision that graph undo and charter history use.
After the commit every daemon is told to drop its cached charter. The next reader resolves the charter from global, team, repo and agent values, in that order.
For a CTO settings change that names a repo, team or agent by name, the gateway turns the name into its settings token, read from the settings_token column of repos, teams or agents.
The setting write starts by reading the current settings revision: the newest revision in setting_history.
It reads all current values. The write is refused if the value the caller expected is no longer the stored one.
The new value is stored for its key, level and scope, with the new revision number. A reset deletes the row.
One history row per changed value keeps the revision, old and new value, author, reason and cause. Undo of a revision reads these rows back.
After the commit the gateway rebuilds the settings snapshot and pushes it to every connected daemon. Daemons and the TUI read the new snapshot and its revision.

journeys.notes: Steps 1 to 5 are the charter change, steps 6 to 12 are the setting change. Both TUI forms and the CTO tools reach the same gateway functions: the TUI charter form and the CTO charter_set tool (inside graph_change) send the frame charter.set (SetLevelCharter in internal/gateway/charter_levels.go); the TUI Settings tab and CTO settings_change send settings.write (internal/gateway/server.go). The TUI Settings tab sends the repo or network address directly and does not read settings_target_identity; step 6 is on the CTO and tool path (internal/daemon/settings.go:readSettings). For a global or team charter the same transaction in setLevelCharter reads and writes charter_values and graph_history, and after the team check reads teams; team purpose, asks_to and lead_merges are team columns written by WriteTeam, not charter_values. When the CTO acts as 'CTO (minor)', graphRecord first runs ctoGraphClassTx, which reads charter_values (maturity) and refuses the change if it is not minor. A charter draft (an agent proposing a charter change) goes another way: SubmitCharterDraft writes charter_drafts and an Inbox ask (inbox_items, charter_draft_asks), and when the owner accepts, DecideCharterDraftRow applies the value with the same write as steps 2 to 4 and sets charter_drafts status to accepted (internal/gateway/charter_drafts.go). Changing delivery.merge_authority or delivery.deploy_rule at repo level may also delete or keep a graph_edges row and add a graph_history row (writeSettingsTx), and a delivery key change calls backfillDeliveryTasks, which can queue approval tasks in delivery_step_tasks. Changing the maturity attribute of a charter also bumps the settings revision. owner_settings did not appear on the normal path: in the settings code I found it only in a one-time cutover migration (settings.go, key cto_settings). The table events gets no row on either path. The old table graph_nodes is still read in parts of the charter code (graphKind, graphRecord for the architect check) and I left it out as instructed.

new_tables.name: plans
new_tables.why: One table for the three kinds of tool and MCP plans.

new_tables.name: oauth_attempts
new_tables.why: One table for the two kinds of OAuth attempt counters.

new_tables.name: gateway_state
new_tables.why: One key and value table for the gateway's own one-off flags and markers. It also took 12 marker rows out of owner_settings, which now holds only settings.

other_moves.what: 12 marker rows moved from owner_settings to gateway_state. They were internal flags, not owner settings.

kept_on_purpose.name: inventory_reports
kept_on_purpose.reason: A machine's inventory is about 630 KB. SQLite rewrites the whole row when any column changes, so with the inventory in nodes each hello went from 50 to 497 microseconds. It stays its own table.

kept_on_purpose.name: delivery_step_inbox
kept_on_purpose.reason: Owner approvals are queued in it with no delivery_step_tasks row (queueOwnerApproval), so it is not a side table of the tasks.

kept_on_purpose.name: pick_candidates
kept_on_purpose.reason: No reader in the gateway. The picker replay tool and the picker research read it from the file.

kept_on_purpose.name: skill_archive_latest
kept_on_purpose.reason: It is a pointer, and not always the highest version.

kept_on_purpose.name: project_bar_next
kept_on_purpose.reason: A counter that stops a deleted rule number from being used again.

kept_on_purpose.name: setting_revision, table_versions
kept_on_purpose.reason: One-row tables read inside transactions or moved by triggers.

kept_on_purpose.name: setting_history, standing_order_history, friction_status_history, skill_archive_changes, skill_list_changes
kept_on_purpose.reason: Each keeps its own typed undo. They do not become one generic history table.

kept_on_purpose.name: profiles, session_checks, worker_usage, worker_assessments
kept_on_purpose.reason: They stay apart from their parent rows.
